newsitem.title: PERU: Thousands of Peruvians march to support hostages.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Peruvians march to support hostages.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Peruvians marched through the streets on Sunday demanding Marxist rebels set free roughly 340 hostages held at the Japanese embassy residence and calling for peaceful dialogue.

In Lima, the mass of marchers dressed in white and and green to symbolise peace and hope arrived within 50 yards (metres) of the besieged compound and chanted to the guerrillas inside to free their captives.
"I know the hostages can feel our support and I want the the terrorists to hear us so that I can have my father back for Christmas," said relative Jose Untama.
The first crowds to approach the residence, hoping to reach the front gate of the compound, jostled for a few minutes with some of a 100 riot police sent to the site to control the march.

One man carried a life-size crucifix on his back and others arranged flowers in a square into the shape of a dove. Four witch doctors danced around an altar of candles, imbibing hallucinogenic potions and chanting "Out with the evil spirits."
"Our march is a show of solidarity with our fellow citizens, the hostages. Violence achieves nothing. We want peace and calm," said Gloria Canales, walking hand-in-hand with her young daughter.
Men and women of all ages sang the national anthem, waved the Peruvian flag and chanted "Peace, peace. Freedom for the hostages."

"With this march, I want them (the hostages) to know that we are with them," said Fernando Andrade, the Miraflores mayor who organised the march from his district only days after dramatically escaping from the residence through a small window.
Around 20 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the residence last Tuesday night, taking hostage a glittering array of international VIPs.
Roofs of the buildings lining the march were also packed with supporters, who joined in the protesters' chants and waved flags while windows were crammed with applauding onlookers.
In Arequipa, Peru's second largest city, the elderly held hands with young children and the able-bodied pushed protesters in wheelchairs.

Up in the Andean highlands at Ayacucho - the city hardest- hit by Peru's 16 wars of guerrilla wars - marchers complaining they were fed up with terrorism sang traditional Indian songs, local radio reported.
A Lima university student, Manuel Chirinos, proudly waving a national flag, said Peru would not give in to the guerrillas' main demand that their jailed comrades be released.
"We want the terrorists to know they are wrong. None of their comrades can or will be released," he said.
Foreigners who had also suffered attacks from the MRTA showed their solidarity with the Peruvians.
"I want to demonstrate my support for peace and the freedom of the hostages," said Rene Carvallo, 47, from Bolivia.
A group of evangelists left their traditional Sunday church service, one carrying a life-size crucifix that carried a message saying: "Gentlemen of the MRTA - reflect."

An 80-strong group of pensioners insisted on completing the two-and-a-half mile (four km-) march together and some even pushed their elderly friends in wheelchairs. "I am a peace-walker," said one 83 year old.

The capital's march also saw an array of famous Peruvians - legislators, artists and actors - mingling in their elegant clothes with ordinary Peruvians who had made the hour-long trip to Miraflores from their humble shanty-towns on the outskirts of the city.
